analysis: A walnut-cased combination barometer, thermometer and clock is a pleasant desk object and the case style points to the 1890-1915 window, but the house has committed to no date at all. Combination instruments were made in quantity and the market for them is thin.
problems: Three mechanisms means three things to be broken, and aneroid movements of this age are almost never accurate. Check the clock runs, the thermometer is unbroken and the barometer needle is not simply painted in place. Restoration is uneconomic at this price.
patience: High. Combination instruments turn up at most general sales.

analysis: A six-piece marble Deco desk set with clock. The form is genuinely of the period but marble desk sets are one of the deadest corners of the Deco market -- heavy, fragile at the corners, and with no practical use left for a blotter and inkwell.
problems: Marble chips and the chips cannot be invisibly repaired. Deco desk clocks of this class are usually cheap French or German movements that no longer run. Six pieces sounds substantial and is why the estimate is what it is.

analysis: A German chiming eight-day mantel clock at $200-300 is the cheapest working-clock proposition in Day 1. Junghans, HAC and Gustav Becker made these by the hundred thousand, so it is common rather than rare, but a chiming movement in a good case is a genuinely useful object.
problems: No maker stated, which for German clocks usually means the backplate stamp was not looked at -- check it, because Becker and Lenzkirch carry a premium over the anonymous makers. Confirm it runs and strikes on the correct hour; a chime out of sequence means a repair bill larger than the clock.
patience: Very high. German mantel clocks are perennially available and perennially cheap.

gems.note: Almost certainly cultured, not natural. Cultured pearl necklaces are the single worst-resale category in jewellery -- a graduated strand that cost $800 new sells for $80-200, and the market has not recovered in thirty years because supply is effectively unlimited. If these were natural pearls the picture reverses entirely, but natural pearls do not carry a $400 estimate.

analysis: A graduated pearl necklace with no period, no origin and no clasp material stated. The catalogue silence is the whole story: an important strand would be described as one.
problems: Pearls also degrade -- nacre wears through at the drill holes and the silk needs restringing every few years. Check the clasp, which is where any gold content would be. The estimate assumes the pearls carry value; they do not.

melt.note: Elgin dress watches of this era are overwhelmingly gold-filled or rolled-gold-plate rather than solid. No melt floor unless the case is marked 14K -- check before assuming anything.

analysis: Elgin was a serious American watchmaker and a vintage Elgin wristwatch at $200-400 is a modest, honest object. The value sits in the movement grade and whether the case is solid gold or filled.
problems: The catalogue says only 'vintage', so no date and no case material. Look for a karat mark inside the caseback -- 'Elgin 10K RGP' or 'gold filled' means the metal is worth nothing. Check it runs; American movements of this era are serviceable but service costs more than the watch.

melt.note: The 'platinum' in the title is an RIAA sales award tier, not a metal. The disc is plated, not platinum. No melt value whatsoever.

analysis: An RIAA award for Billy Squier's Don't Say No. This is music memorabilia, not jewellery and not a precious metal object, and it fits none of the five criteria. Value depends entirely on the artist's standing and Squier is a second-tier name.
problems: RIAA awards are also the most faked category in music memorabilia -- reproduction plaques are made to order. Genuine ones have specific RIAA hologram and engraving conventions by era. Five of these run consecutively at 1323-1327, which is a consignment.

analysis: A Taino stone fetish pendant. If genuine this is a pre-Columbian Caribbean antiquity, which is far older than anything else in the sale -- but antiquities are a category where authenticity and legal title matter more than age.
problems: Two serious problems. Taino material is extensively faked for the tourist and collector trade, and carved stone is nearly impossible to authenticate visually. More importantly, pre-Columbian antiquities are subject to import and patrimony restrictions, and a lot at this price will carry no provenance documentation. Ask what its collection history is; if the answer is vague, walk.
patience: High -- and the authenticity risk means patience costs you nothing here.

analysis: Chelsea Clock Company of Boston is the best American marine clock maker and its US Navy deck clocks are properly collected. A 24-hour dial is the less common variant -- Navy deck clocks were made in both 12- and 24-hour configurations and the 24-hour ones read as more obviously military. At $500-700 this is fair rather than cheap, but Chelsea holds value better than almost any clock in this sale.
problems: Confirm the movement is Chelsea's own and matches the case, and that the serial number on the movement is present -- Chelsea will date a movement from it, which converts an inferred date into a documented one. Bakelite and phenolic cases of this era crack at the bezel. Check it runs; Chelsea service is available but not cheap.
patience: Moderate. Chelsea deck clocks appear regularly in marine sales but this is the bottom of their range.

analysis: Joseph Sewill of Liverpool was a first-rank chronometer and ship's clock maker, and a US Army ship's clock by him is a genuinely interesting cross-service object. This is good material.
problems: It is also $1,000-1,500 with a $500 opening, comfortably outside the budget band -- $1,320 to $1,980 all-in. Noted rather than screened because it is the best clock in Day 2 and worth seeing at preview, but bidding it means abandoning the discipline.

analysis: A WWII-era Chelsea US Navy Mark I deck clock. The same maker as 2014 and the same quality, but the Mark I 12-hour pattern is the common one -- these were produced in quantity for the wartime fleet. Note that 2056 is a second identical example: two of the same clock in one sale is the classic setup where the second goes cheaper.
problems: Watch both 2044 and 2056 and bid whichever the room leaves alone. Same checks as 2014: matching serial, running movement, uncracked bezel. Wartime cases were often repainted in service, which is honest wear rather than damage.
patience: High. Mark I deck clocks are the commonest Chelsea military model.

analysis: The second of two identical WWII Chelsea Mark I deck clocks, twelve lots after the first. Being the later of a duplicate pair is a real advantage: whoever wanted a Chelsea deck clock has already bought one by the time this crosses the block.
problems: Identical checks to 2044. If both go past $560, the room has a Chelsea collector in it and there is no point competing.
patience: High, and improved by having two chances at the same object.

melt.basis: pair-case silver watch case only; movement, dial and glass are not silver

analysis: Morris Tobias and Levitt were established London makers and an English silver verge fusee is a genuinely antique, genuinely mechanical object -- the last generation of hand-made watchmaking before the lever escapement. Eight photographs suggests the movement is being shown properly.
problems: At $1,500-2,000 with a $750 opening it is well outside the band. The silver case holds only about $110-165 of metal, so the estimate is entirely horological value -- which is real but illiquid, since verge fusees sell to a small specialist audience. Worth examining at preview for the education.

analysis: An English tall case clock with moon phase dial, signed Edward Glase of Bridgnorth and catalogued circa 1800. A signed provincial longcase with a moon phase is a proper antique and the date is the house's stated claim.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-2,500 with a $1,000 opening. Beyond price: longcase clocks are the most married objects in furniture -- movements, dials and cases are routinely recombined, and a signed dial in a case that never held it is common. It is also seven feet of object needing a level floor.

melt.basis: CAUTION -- Turkoman tribal silver is usually well below sterling, often .600 to .800, and sometimes silver-washed base metal. Costed at sterling as the optimistic case; assume less and expect a refiner to discount tribal alloy harder than the usual 87%.

gems.note: Carnelian is abundant and cheap. No meaningful recoverable value.

analysis: Two Turkoman silver and carnelian pendants. Central Asian tribal silver has a genuine following and the workmanship is often better than the price suggests, but this is bought as ethnographic ornament rather than as metal or as antique.
problems: Purity is the issue -- test it rather than assuming. Turkoman work is also reproduced in quantity in Afghanistan and Pakistan for the export trade, and the reproductions use the same forms and stones. Period pieces show wear at the suspension loops and a soft, uneven patina in the recesses.
patience: High. Tribal silver appears regularly and cheaply.

melt.basis: pair of cuffs; Kabyle silver runs well below sterling, so treat this as the ceiling not the expectation

analysis: A pair of Algerian Kabyle silver and enamel cuff bracelets. Berber enamel work is a distinctive and properly collected tradition and a matched pair is better than a single.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-2,500 with a $1,000 opening. The silver holds perhaps $135-225 at best, so the estimate is entirely the ethnographic and enamel value. Kabyle enamel chips and losses are near-universal and expensive to stabilise.

melt.basis: beads and silver elements; Moroccan silver is commonly .800 or lower, so this is the optimistic case

analysis: A Moroccan silver and bead necklace at $200-300 -- the cheapest of the North African group. Bought as wearable ethnographic ornament; there is no antique claim and no named maker.
problems: Test the silver. 'Bead' in the title is doing work -- glass, resin and plastic beads are all common in this material and none has value. Modern tourist-trade pieces are indistinguishable from older ones in photographs.

melt.basis: single pendant; assume sub-sterling alloy

gems.note: Enamel only -- decorative, nothing recoverable, and chips are common.

analysis: A Moroccan silver and enamel triangular pendant. The triangular khamsa-adjacent form is characteristic and the enamel work is what carries the interest.
problems: Same purity and modernity questions as the rest of the North African group. Check the enamel for losses and the reverse for a modern soldered pin or jump ring, which indicates a piece assembled for the export market.

melt.basis: two small pendants; sub-sterling alloy likely

analysis: Two North African silver amulet pendants at $200-300. The cheapest way into this material and, being a pair, the one with the most to look at.
problems: Amulet cases were often made to hold a written charm and are frequently empty or opened -- check whether they are intact. Purity untested, date unstated, origin given only as 'North African', which is the vaguest attribution in the group.

melt.basis: mounts and clasp only -- the jadeite is the bulk of the object and is not metal

gems.note: Jadeite is the entire question and its value range is enormous. Translucent, evenly coloured 'Type A' untreated jadeite is worth many multiples of the gold; opaque, dyed or polymer-impregnated 'Type B/C' material is worth almost nothing and is extremely common. This cannot be settled from a photograph -- it needs a loupe and ideally a refractometer or a lab note.

analysis: A two-piece Chinese carved 14K gold and jadeite suite at $600-800 is inside the band, and the gold alone is roughly $450-900 -- so the metal nearly covers the estimate before the stone counts for anything. That makes it a reasonable floor with genuine upside if the jade is good.
problems: The jade is the whole variable and dyed jadeite is the single most common deception in Chinese jewellery. Look for colour concentrated in fractures rather than distributed through the stone, and for the slightly glassy, too-even green of polymer treatment. Treat the gold as the value and the jade as a free option.
patience: Moderate. Jadeite suites appear regularly but ones where the gold covers the estimate are less common.

analysis: A single Chinese Warring States necklace bead. If genuine it is well over two thousand years old, which is remarkable, and at $300-500 it would be cheap for that.
problems: That is exactly the problem. Warring States and Han glass and stone beads are reproduced in enormous quantity in China specifically for the antiquities trade, and a single loose bead has no context to authenticate it against. There is also no provenance for an object that would need one. The catalogue's own typo -- 'WARRING STATED' -- does not suggest specialist cataloguing.
patience: Irrelevant -- the authenticity risk is the whole story.

analysis: A Gruen watch shop advertising clock from Chelsea, Massachusetts. Double-sided advertising clocks from jewellers' shopfronts are a strong category -- they sit at the intersection of horology, advertising and signage collecting -- and the named Massachusetts town gives it a specific New England history. At $300-400 this is the best-value clock in Day 3.
problems: Advertising clocks are reproduced heavily for the decorating trade and the Gruen name is one of the copied ones. Period examples show a genuine electric or spring movement of the era, screen-printed rather than digitally printed glass or metal, and honest wear on the mounting bracket. Check whether it is a genuine shop clock or a modern reproduction dial in an old case.
patience: Low to moderate. Named-shop advertising clocks are genuinely less common than the general run of advertising material.

analysis: A pair of Urban Archeology cargo pendant lights. These are contemporary reproduction industrial fixtures from a high-end New York lighting firm, not antiques and not jewellery -- the word 'pendant' is doing the misleading work here.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-3,000. Urban Archeology fixtures retail for several thousand new, so the estimate is a discount on retail rather than an antique valuation, and resale on contemporary lighting is poor because the buyer can simply order new.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band and out of criteria.

melt.basis: articulated abacus pendant -- these are substantial because the frame and beads are all gold

analysis: A 14K gold abacus pendant with working beads. Worth noting precisely because the melt is close to the estimate: at 14 to 20 grams the gold is roughly $1,050 to $1,500 against a $1,200-1,500 estimate. That means almost no premium is being asked for the novelty, which is unusual in this section.
problems: Out of band -- $1,200 hammer is $1,584 all-in. Weigh it before believing the melt figure; abacus pendants vary a lot in substance and a hollow-frame example would hold far less gold. If it somehow fell to $900 it would be a metal buy.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, but the melt parity is worth knowing.

melt.note: Platinum. The brief supplies no working platinum rate, and I will not invent one -- if this mattered you would need a current neutral quote. Note that platinum scrap recovery is notably worse than gold: refiners pay a lower percentage and platinum has traded below gold for years, so a platinum mount is not the metal floor people assume.

gems.note: Diamond and sapphire in a Deco ring. Secondary-market recovery on small stones is 25-40% of retail at best, and period sapphires are frequently heat-treated. The Deco design is worth more than the stones.

analysis: A genuine period Art Deco platinum, diamond and sapphire ring. Deco is the one twentieth-century style where original design carries a real premium over the materials, and this is authentic rather than revival.
problems: Out of band at $1,500-2,000 with a $750 opening. Also worth knowing: platinum Deco mounts are brittle after a century and hairline cracks at the shoulders are common and hard to repair well.

melt.basis: spray brooch, stones deducted

gems.note: Small diamonds in a floral spray -- melee and near-melee, which recover very little. The gold is the substance.

analysis: A Dan Frere 14K gold and diamond flower spray brooch. The gold is roughly $900-1,350, so the $1,500-1,800 estimate carries a modest premium over metal for the maker and the diamonds.
problems: Out of band. Dan Frere is a minor mid-century American maker rather than a name that commands a premium, so this is close to a metal-plus-a-little proposition at an above-metal price.

melt.basis: necklace and pendant mount, stones and pearls deducted

gems.note: Sapphire, pearl and diamond. Edwardian pearls in jewellery of this class are often natural rather than cultured, which would matter -- but it needs testing, and the seed pearls typical of the style are individually worth little.

analysis: An Edwardian 14K gold, sapphire, pearl and diamond pendant necklace -- one of the few genuinely period pieces in the Day 3 jewellery run, sitting right on the antique line. Edwardian design is delicate and undervalued relative to Deco.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-3,000. Edwardian settings are fine to the point of fragility; check the gallery work and knife-edge wires for previous repairs, and whether the seed pearls are complete -- missing pearls are near-universal and replacement is fiddly.

melt.basis: rose brooch, stones deducted; floral brooches of this size are solid rather than hollow

gems.note: Small diamond and sapphire accents. Recovery is minimal -- treat them as decoration, not value.

analysis: This is the one to actually buy in the Day 3 jewellery run. A 14K gold diamond and sapphire rose brooch estimated $500-700 with a $100 opening, and on my weight estimate the gold alone is roughly $450 to $750. The metal covers the estimate, which means the design and stones come free and the downside is the refiner's price.
problems: Weigh it -- the entire case rests on the gold being solid at 6 to 10 grams, and a thin stamped brooch would hold half that. Check the pin and catch, which are the usual failure points and are sometimes base metal even on a gold brooch. Confirm the 14K mark.
patience: Moderate. Gold floral brooches are common, but ones estimated at or below their own melt are not -- this is a function of gold at $4,000 an ounce rather than anything special about the brooch.

melt.basis: line bracelet, stones deducted

gems.note: A Deco line bracelet's diamonds are individually small but numerous; as a set they carry more than melee usually would. Sapphires of the period are commonly heat-treated.

analysis: A genuine Art Deco 14K gold, diamond and sapphire line bracelet. The gold is roughly $1,350-2,100 and the stones add real value on top, so the $3,000-5,000 estimate is not unreasonable for authentic period Deco.
problems: Comprehensively out of band at three to five times the ceiling. Line bracelets also fail at the links; check every hinge and the safety catch, because a broken Deco bracelet is an expensive repair.

melt.basis: dogwood flower necklace, stones deducted

gems.note: Small diamonds. Minimal recovery.

analysis: An HSB 14K gold and diamond dogwood flower necklace. The gold is roughly $750 to $1,200 against an $800-1,200 estimate, so like several lots in this run the metal essentially covers the ask -- a consequence of the working gold price rather than a bargain in the design.
problems: Only just inside the band at the low estimate and outside it above $1,000 hammer. HSB is not a name that adds value. Weigh it; a necklace with fine chain and small flower heads may hold much less gold than the design suggests.
patience: High. Gold floral necklaces are abundant.

melt.basis: grape cluster brooch, pearls deducted

gems.note: Cultured pearls forming the grape cluster -- effectively no resale value. If pearls are missing, that is cosmetic only.

analysis: A 14K gold and pearl grape cluster brooch, estimated $700-900 against roughly $600-900 of gold. Another lot where the metal underwrites most of the price. The grape cluster is a durable mid-century form that still wears well.
problems: Inside the band and the melt is close to the estimate, so the risk is low -- but so is the upside. Check whether the pearls are original and intact, and weigh the gold rather than trusting the apparent bulk of a clustered design.

melt.basis: pill box; small gold boxes are surprisingly heavy because the walls and hinge are solid

analysis: An antique 14K gold monogrammed pill box. The gold is roughly $1,500 to $2,250 against a $2,000-2,500 estimate -- so this is very close to a pure metal proposition with the antique interest thrown in. Note the monogram, which the market discounts and this buyer should not care about.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-2,500. 'Antique' is unverified with no date and no maker. Weigh it and check the hinge, which on gold boxes is sometimes a base-metal insert that must be deducted.

melt.basis: Peretti's designs are characteristically smooth and solid rather than hollow

analysis: An Elsa Peretti for Tiffany 18K gold starfish brooch. Peretti is one of the few designer names where the signature genuinely adds to the metal, and 18K at $96.45 a gram puts the gold at roughly $1,150 to $1,930 -- at or above the $1,200-1,500 estimate.
problems: Out of band. Peretti pieces are also faked, so confirm the Tiffany and Peretti marks are correct in form and placement rather than merely present.

melt.basis: brooch body

analysis: A Paloma Picasso for Tiffany 18K gold brooch -- the companion to the Peretti two lots earlier and the same logic. Roughly $1,060 to $1,740 of gold against a $1,200-1,500 estimate, so the metal underwrites it and the designer name is close to free.
problems: Out of band. Same mark-authentication point as the Peretti.

melt.basis: 18K portions only; the platinum elements are not costed as the brief gives no platinum rate

gems.note: Jade, amethyst and diamond. Amethyst is worth almost nothing; the jade is the variable and needs the same Type A/B/C assessment as lot 2498.

analysis: A Carrington & Co. 18K gold, platinum, jade, amethyst and diamond thistle brooch. Carrington was a good American maker and a thistle in mixed materials is an attractive, well-made object.
problems: Out of band at $2,000-3,000. The mixed construction makes the metal hard to value -- you cannot weigh the gold separately from the platinum without dismantling it, so treat the melt figure as indicative only.

melt.basis: ring shank and head, stone deducted

gems.note: The diamond is the whole value here -- the gold is only $225-450. With no carat weight, colour or clarity stated, the estimate is unpriceable. A $2,000-3,000 estimate implies roughly a one-carat stone; secondary-market recovery on that is typically 30-40% of retail.

analysis: A 14K rose gold and diamond ring with no stone specification whatsoever -- no carat weight, no colour, no clarity, and only one photograph.
problems: Out of band, and the catalogue tells you nothing you would need to bid intelligently. When a diamond ring carries a four-figure estimate and no stone details, the details are being withheld or were never taken. Do not bid blind on stones.

melt.basis: figural brooch, stones deducted

gems.note: Small diamonds and rubies as accents. Rubies of this class are commonly synthetic or heavily treated.

analysis: A George Lederman 18K gold, diamond and ruby shark brooch. A figural novelty in solid 18K, so roughly $1,160 to $1,930 of gold against a $1,500-2,500 estimate.
problems: Out of band. Figural novelty jewellery has a narrow audience -- a shark brooch appeals to whoever wants a shark brooch, and that is a thin market on resale even though the metal holds.

melt.basis: band ring, stones deducted; band rings are heavier than solitaire mounts

gems.note: An unspecified number of diamonds in a band. Channel- or pave-set melee, which recovers very little individually.

analysis: A 14K gold and diamond band ring. Gold is roughly $375 to $675, so the $1,200-1,800 estimate is mostly stone value -- and the stones are unspecified.
problems: Out of band, and again no stone detail. Diamond bands are also the hardest jewellery to resell because size cannot be altered much without disturbing the setting.

melt.basis: pendant mount, stones deducted

gems.note: The star ruby is the entire question and the range is why this is CHECK FIRST. A natural star ruby of decent size and sharp asterism is worth several hundred; a Linde synthetic star ruby -- mass-produced from the 1940s and extremely common in mid-century American jewellery -- is worth $20-40. They look very similar to the naked eye.

analysis: A 14K gold star ruby and diamond pendant estimated $800-1,200 against only $300-530 of gold. That means the estimate is a bet on the ruby, and the ruby is exactly what cannot be judged from two photographs.
problems: Synthetic star rubies are the single most common trap in mid-century American jewellery, and the giveaway is a too-perfect six-rayed star with unnaturally even legs, plus curved growth lines under magnification. Get a loupe on it at preview. If it is Linde, this is a $250 object.
patience: High. Star ruby pendants are abundant and mostly synthetic.

melt.basis: floral brooch in multiple gold colours, stones deducted

gems.note: Small diamond accents only.

analysis: A 14K multi-colour gold and diamond floral brooch, estimated $800-1,000 against roughly $600 to $1,050 of gold. Multi-colour gold work uses rose, white and yellow alloys and tends to be solidly made, which helps the weight.
problems: Right at the top of the budget band, so there is little room. Weigh it. Multi-colour gold is also harder to sell than plain yellow because the look is dated, which is why the resale range sits close to melt rather than above it.

melt.basis: brooch/pendant body less the seed pearls and diamond

gems.note: Seed pearls have essentially no individual value and are frequently missing; the single diamond is small. The interest is the period design, not the stones.

analysis: An antique 14K gold, diamond and seed pearl brooch/pendant at $700-900. The gold is roughly $375 to $675, so unlike most of this run the estimate sits above melt -- but here you are buying genuine period design rather than metal, and a piece that converts between brooch and pendant is more wearable and more saleable than either alone.
problems: 'Antique' is unverified with no date, though the seed pearl and diamond combination points firmly at 1890-1915. Count the seed pearls against the settings: missing pearls are the standard condition fault and each empty cup is a small deduction. Check the pendant fitting and the pin are both intact and original.
patience: Moderate. Convertible Edwardian brooch-pendants appear regularly but this is at the sensible end of the price range.

melt.basis: Turk's head is a woven rope knot in solid 18K -- these are very heavy

analysis: Worth flagging despite the price because A.G.A. Correa is a Maine maker -- Wiscasset, on Route 1, twenty minutes from Bath -- and the Turk's head knot is their signature nautical design. It is the only lot in the jewellery run with a genuine Maine connection. The gold is roughly $5,800 to $9,200, so the estimate is metal plus a real maker premium.
problems: Ten to twelve thousand dollars is ten times the budget ceiling. Included so the Maine connection is on the record rather than missed, not as a suggestion.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band. Correa is still trading, so their work is available new.

melt.basis: three-stone ring mount

gems.note: Diamond and sapphire three-stone. No carat weights given, so unpriceable -- the estimate implies substantial stones.

analysis: A 14K gold diamond and sapphire three-stone ring. The gold is only $300-530; everything else in the $3,000-5,000 estimate is stone value that the catalogue does not specify.
problems: Out of band and undocumented. Three-stone rings are also where treated and synthetic sapphires are most often found paired with modest diamonds.

melt.basis: torsade clasp and gold elements; the pearls are the bulk and are not metal

gems.note: Cultured pearls, almost certainly. A multi-strand torsade looks impressive and recovers poorly -- pearl resale is the weakest in the trade.

analysis: An Italian 18K gold and pearl torsade necklace. Italian gold work of this type is solidly made and the gold could run $2,900 to $5,300, which underwrites much of the estimate.
problems: Out of band. And be clear-eyed about the pearls: they carry the visual bulk and almost none of the value, which is why my resale range sits well under the estimate.

melt.basis: pendant mount only

gems.note: Three diamonds carrying essentially the whole value, with no carat weights, colour or clarity stated and a single photograph.

analysis: A 14K gold three-stone diamond pendant necklace. The gold is $225-450 against a $4,000-6,000 estimate, so this is a diamond lot in a gold wrapper.
problems: Out of band, and one photograph for a four-figure diamond lot is inadequate disclosure. Never bid this class of lot without either a lab report or your own loupe on the stones.

melt.basis: white gold cluster mount

gems.note: Ruby and diamond cluster. Cluster rings are where treated rubies concentrate -- glass-filled and lead-treated stones are endemic in this price class and are worth a fraction of untreated material.

analysis: An 18K white gold ruby and diamond cluster ring. Gold is $385-770; the rest of the $3,000-4,000 estimate is stones of unstated quality.
problems: Out of band. Ruby treatment disclosure is the specific risk -- ask directly whether the stones have been assessed, and assume treated if nobody will say.

melt.note: Platinum -- no working rate in the brief, and platinum scrap recovery is poor. The value here is entirely the diamonds.

gems.note: A substantial diamond spray brooch. This is the most valuable single lot in the jewellery run and its value is almost entirely the stones.

analysis: A vintage platinum and diamond spray brooch at $15,000-20,000 -- fifteen to twenty times the budget ceiling and the most expensive jewellery lot in the sale.
problems: Recorded for completeness. Two photographs for a five-figure diamond lot is thin, and at this level you would want a lab report before bidding.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

melt.basis: case and integrated bracelet if present; movement and dial are not gold

analysis: A Cartier 18K gold woman's cocktail wristwatch. Cartier is the one watch name here where the signature reliably adds to the metal, and the gold is roughly $1,450 to $2,400.
problems: Out of band at $3,000-5,000. Cartier is also the most counterfeited fine-watch brand -- confirm the movement, the serial and the case marks, and be aware that redialled Cartiers are common. Only two photographs.

melt.note: Platinum -- no working rate, and poor scrap recovery. Value is the stones.

gems.note: Three diamonds, unspecified. The whole value.

analysis: A platinum three-stone diamond ring, unspecified as to stone weight or quality. One of four essentially interchangeable three-stone diamond rings in this run (3118, 3120, 3124, 3230).
problems: Out of band, and no stone documentation. The repetition across the run suggests a single jewellery consignment being dispersed.

melt.basis: CANNOT BE COSTED FROM THE TITLE. Cross made both solid-14K and 14K-gold-FILLED pens, and the two look identical. Solid: 12-18 g of gold, roughly $900-1,350. Filled: no melt floor at all. The zero at the bottom of the range is the honest lower bound.

analysis: A Cross 14K gold pen and pencil set in its original box, estimated $600-800 -- inside the band. Whether this is a good buy or a bad one depends entirely on one thing the catalogue does not say: solid or filled.
problems: This is the single most important thing to check in the jewellery run because the answer swings the lot from roughly $1,000 of gold to roughly $80 of writing instrument. Look for '14K' alone (solid) versus '14K gold filled', '1/20 14K' or 'GF' (not solid). Cross marked its barrels near the cap band. If nobody can tell you, assume filled.
patience: High. Cross sets are common; solid gold ones much less so.

melt.basis: pair of earrings

analysis: A pair of 18K gold earrings attributed to Lapponia. Lapponia is the Finnish modernist house Bjorn Weckstrom worked for and genuine pieces carry a design premium; the gold is roughly $770 to $1,350.
problems: Out of band, and note 'attributed to' -- per the standing principles that is a hopeful label rather than an attribution. Lapponia marked its work clearly, so an attributed piece is one where the mark is absent or unreadable. Price it as anonymous 18K, which is roughly melt.

melt.basis: necklace, stones deducted

gems.note: Tourmaline is attractive and cheap -- good specimens are affordable and recovery is modest. The diamonds are accents.

analysis: A 14K gold tourmaline and diamond necklace. Gold is $600-1,130 against a $3,000-5,000 estimate, so the stones are being valued highly for a species that is not expensive.
problems: Out of band, and the estimate looks optimistic relative to what tourmaline actually recovers. This is the kind of lot where the house estimate is doing the work.

melt.basis: geometric brooch, stones deducted

gems.note: Pave or channel-set diamonds, unspecified.

analysis: An 18K white gold and diamond geometric brooch. Gold is roughly $965 to $1,740 against $3,000-4,000.
problems: Out of band. White gold also needs rhodium replating every few years to stay white, which is a small recurring cost that suppresses resale slightly.

melt.basis: multi-strand bracelet, stones deducted -- substantial gold

gems.note: Numerous small diamonds.

analysis: An 18K gold multi-strand diamond bracelet. The gold is roughly $2,400 to $3,860, which underwrites a good share of the $4,500-5,500 estimate.
problems: Out of band. Multi-strand bracelets fail at the strand attachments; check each one and the clasp.

melt.basis: rose gold ring mount, stones deducted

gems.note: Aquamarine is abundant and inexpensive; the diamonds are accents. Neither recovers much.

analysis: An 18K rose gold aquamarine and diamond ring. Gold is $385-675, so the $1,000-1,500 estimate leans on an aquamarine, which is one of the cheaper coloured stones per carat.
problems: Marginal on band at the low estimate and out of it above $1,000. The stone species does not support the estimate in my view -- this is a case where I read the market lower than the house.

melt.basis: brooch body, stones deducted

gems.note: Unspecified diamonds.

analysis: An 18K gold and diamond brooch with no further description at all. Gold roughly $965 to $1,545 against a $1,500-1,800 estimate, so metal plus a modest premium.
problems: Out of band. A catalogue entry this bare -- no design, no maker, no period -- is why the lot will sell on metal.

melt.note: Platinum -- no working rate, poor scrap recovery.

gems.note: Three diamonds, unspecified. The third of four near-identical three-stone rings in the run.

analysis: A platinum and diamond three-stone ring, estimated $2,500-3,000. Interchangeable with 3118, 3124 and 3230 as far as the catalogue reveals.
problems: Out of band, no stone detail. Four comparable three-stone rings in one sale will compete with each other, which is useful information if you ever did want one -- but not at these estimates.

melt.basis: a suite -- necklace plus earrings and possibly bracelet, so substantial gold

gems.note: Unspecified diamonds across the suite.

analysis: An 18K gold and diamond Greek key design jewellery suite. The gold could run $4,340 to $7,230, which is most of the $8,000-10,000 estimate.
problems: Far out of band, and a single photograph for a suite is poor disclosure -- you cannot even confirm how many pieces are included.
